title: Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol
summary: Describes an updated version of the security architecture for IP, which provides security services for traffic at the IP layer. It explains how IPsec components fit together and replaces RFC 2401. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: IPsec adds security at the IP layer, so every protocol that runs over IP is protected, not just one application. RFC 4301 is the architecture document: it defines the components of IPsec, the databases that hold policy and keys, and how each inbound and outbound packet is handled.

subtitle: The blueprint for IPsec: how security associations and three databases decide which IP packets get protected, dropped or passed through.

tldr.problem: IP by itself offers no protection. Hosts and gateways need a standard way to authenticate, protect and filter traffic at the IP layer, for both IPv4 and IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: IPsec places a boundary between protected and unprotected interfaces. A policy database decides per packet whether to PROTECT, DISCARD or BYPASS. Protected traffic travels over security associations that use ESP or AH.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4301 obsoletes RFC 2401. It is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 6040 and RFC 7619.

today: RFC 4301 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2401. It updates RFC 3168 and has been updated by RFC 6040 and RFC 7619.

sections.title: Goals of the IPsec Architecture
sections.content:
RFC 4301 specifies the base architecture for IPsec-compliant systems. It describes the requirements for systems that implement IPsec, the fundamental elements of such systems, and how they fit together and into the IP environment, for both IPv4 and IPv6. Other RFCs define the individual protocols and algorithms.

The security services are access control, connectionless integrity, data origin authentication, detection and rejection of replays, confidentiality through encryption, and limited traffic flow confidentiality. Because these services work at the IP layer, they protect every protocol carried over IP. The spelling IPsec is the preferred one.

IPsec includes minimal firewall functionality, since that is an essential part of access control at the IP layer. The protocols are designed to be independent of cryptographic algorithms. The default algorithms are specified in separate documents, so they can be updated without reopening the architecture.

The RFC is explicit about limits. This is not a security architecture for the Internet, only for the IP layer. The security achieved also depends on the quality of the implementation and on the operating environment.

This document replaces RFC 2401. The fundamental ideas are unchanged, but the processing model was revised to cover new scenarios, improve performance and simplify implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec protects traffic at the IP layer. That covers every protocol that runs over IP, not just one application. RFC 4301 defines the pieces of an IPsec system, the databases they use, and the rules each packet is checked against. It covers both IPv4 and IPv6. Other documents define the individual protocols.

sections.title: How IPsec Works: Boundary, Protocols and Placement
sections.content:
An IPsec implementation sits in a host, in a security gateway (SG) such as an IPsec-enabled firewall or router, or in an independent device. It creates a boundary between unprotected and protected interfaces. Each packet crossing it is matched against the Security Policy Database (SPD) using selectors and receives one of three actions: PROTECT it with IPsec, DISCARD it, or BYPASS IPsec protection.

Two protocols provide protection. The Authentication Header (AH) offers integrity and data origin authentication with optional anti-replay. The Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) offers the same services and also confidentiality. Implementations MUST support ESP and MAY support AH, because experience showed that ESP can provide the needed services in nearly all contexts. ESP confidentiality without integrity is NOT RECOMMENDED.

Implementation can be native in the IP stack, bump-in-the-stack (BITS) beneath an existing stack, or bump-in-the-wire (BITW) as a dedicated inline processor. The document assumes IKEv2, or a key management system with comparable features, for automated setup of security associations.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPsec implementation draws a line between protected and unprotected network interfaces. Every packet that crosses that line is checked against a policy database. The packet is then protected, dropped, or passed through unchanged. Two protocols do the protecting: ESP, which can also encrypt, and AH, which only authenticates. ESP is required; AH is optional.

sections.title: Security Associations and Modes
sections.content:
A Security Association (SA) is a simplex, one-way connection that provides security services to the traffic it carries, using AH or ESP but not both. Two-way communication therefore needs a pair of SAs, one per direction, and IKE creates such pairs. For unicast, the 32-bit Security Parameters Index (SPI) by itself can identify an SA. Multicast needs a defined lookup order: SPI plus destination and source addresses, then SPI plus destination, then SPI alone or SPI and protocol.

An SA operates in one of two modes. In transport mode the security header sits right after the IP header and protects the next layer protocol. ESP in this mode does not cover the IP header. In tunnel mode the SA is applied to an IP tunnel, with an outer header naming the tunnel endpoints and an inner header naming the original sender and recipient. When either end is a security gateway, the SA MUST be tunnel mode, with narrow exceptions such as traffic addressed to the gateway itself.

Traffic of different classes that match the same selectors should travel on different SAs when anti-replay is used. Otherwise the anti-replay window could wrongly discard lower priority packets. The RFC also notes that AH and ESP cannot be applied in transport mode to IPv4 fragments.
sections.plainLanguage: A security association is a one-way protected connection between two peers. Each direction needs its own association, so a conversation uses a pair. Every association is identified by a 32-bit number called the SPI. An association works in one of two modes: transport mode protects the payload of an existing packet, while tunnel mode wraps the whole packet in a new outer header.

sections.title: The Three IPsec Databases
sections.content:
The SPD is an ordered policy database. Each entry names a disposition (PROTECT, BYPASS or DISCARD) and is keyed by selectors. The selectors include local and remote IP address ranges, next layer protocol, and ports, ICMP type and code, or Mobility Header type when relevant. Values can be a range, ANY, or OPAQUE when a field is unavailable, as in a non-initial fragment. The SPD is logically divided into SPD-S (secure traffic), SPD-I (inbound bypass or discard) and SPD-O (outbound bypass or discard). Every SPD SHOULD end with a final entry that discards anything unmatched.

The Security Association Database (SAD) holds the parameters of each SA. These include the SPI, a sequence number counter (64-bit by default), an anti-replay window, algorithms and keys, lifetime by time and byte count, mode, and path MTU. For inbound packets, the SAD also acts as a cache for checking that header fields match the selectors negotiated for the SA.

The Peer Authorization Database (PAD) links the SPD to a key management protocol such as IKE. It identifies authorized peers, states how each is authenticated and with what data, and limits which identities a peer may assert when child SAs are created.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec uses three databases. The SPD holds the policy: for each kind of traffic it says protect, drop, or pass through. The SAD holds the settings of every live security association, including keys and sequence numbers. The PAD lists which peers are allowed to negotiate associations and how each peer proves its identity.

sections.title: SA and Key Management
sections.content:
All IPsec implementations MUST support both manual and automated SA and key management. Manual keying means a person configures keying material by hand. It works for small, static settings but does not scale. Automated management is required to use anti-replay and to create SAs on demand. Rekeying an SA means creating a new SA with a new SPI.

The default automated protocol is IKEv2. Other automated protocols MAY be used. One negotiation yields several keys for an SA, and a minimum of four are needed when both integrity and confidentiality are used, because each direction has its own SA. When a single bit string is split into keys, encryption keys MUST come from the first (left-most, high-order) bits and integrity keys from the remaining bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Security associations and their keys can be set up by hand or by a protocol. Hand setup works for a few static tunnels. A protocol such as IKEv2 is needed for larger deployments and for features that need fresh keys. When one shared secret is cut into several keys, both sides must cut it the same way.

sections.title: Processing Outbound and Inbound Traffic
sections.content:
For outbound packets, IPsec picks the right SPD through an SPD selection function, matches the packet against the SPD cache, and acts on the entry. A cache miss means a search of the SPD. If the entry says PROTECT and no SA exists, the key management mechanism, such as IKEv2, is invoked to create one. If creation fails, the packet is discarded. The packet then goes to the forwarding function, which may loop it back across the boundary for nested processing, and that needs a matching SPD-I entry.

For inbound packets, traffic that looks IPsec protected and is addressed to the device is mapped to an SA through the SAD using the SPI. Everything else goes to an SPD-I lookup. IKE traffic MUST have an explicit BYPASS entry.

For tunnel mode, the outer header addresses identify the tunnel endpoints, and the inner header is left unchanged apart from fields such as TTL and the DS and ECN fields. IPsec tunnel mode differs from plain IP-in-IP tunneling by adding controls that limit how much header data can pass across the boundary, which narrows covert channels. Handling of the DSCP value on the outer header is a security-relevant choice: copying it can leak information about the inner traffic.

ICMP error messages need special care. An error message that maps to no existing SA must be carried on the SA that would carry the return traffic for the packet that triggered the error, by reversing the addresses and ports found in the ICMP payload. On receipt, an ICMP error message whose outer headers do not match the SA selectors must be checked against the triggering packet header inside the payload; if that check fails, the message is dropped and the event is auditable. Otherwise a host could be tricked into believing that parts of a protected network are unreachable.
sections.plainLanguage: Going out, the implementation checks the policy database, finds or creates a security association, and applies it. Coming in, it uses the SPI on the packet to find the right association, then checks that the packet matches what that association allows. ICMP error messages are checked against the packet that caused them, so a forged error cannot be used to black-hole protected traffic.

sections.title: Fragments, Path MTU and Auditing
sections.content:
IP fragmentation interacts badly with the selectors used for access control, because a non-initial fragment does not carry the ports, ICMP type and code, or sometimes even the next layer protocol. RFC 4301 gives three approaches for plaintext fragments on the protected side. Tunnel mode SAs that ignore port fields can carry all fragments for given addresses and protocols. Separate tunnel mode SAs can carry only non-initial fragments, with the port selectors set to OPAQUE; receivers MUST then apply a minimum offset check on IPv4 fragments to resist overlapping fragment attacks. Or the implementation can negotiate stateful fragment checking, in which case the peer is told with the NON_FIRST_FRAGMENTS_ALSO notify payload and non-initial fragments on a port-specific SA are discarded unless that feature was agreed. Transport mode SAs never carry fragments.

BYPASS and DISCARD traffic needs matching care. Cleartext non-initial fragments that overlap protected traffic could undermine its integrity, so implementations MUST support stateful fragment checking for BYPASS entries that specify a non-trivial port range.

Applying AH or ESP makes packets larger, which can push them over the path MTU of the SA. Each SA carries a path MTU value that is updated from ICMP PMTU messages and must be aged, typically by periodically resetting it to the first-hop data-link MTU and letting discovery run again. The DF bit on tunnel mode SAs can be set, cleared or copied from the inner header, and this is configurable per SA. IPv6 packets may only be fragmented by the originator.

Auditing is not required, but the RFC lists auditable events, such as dropping an ICMP error that fails the consistency check, and defines a minimum set of information for each. A receiver MUST NOT send a message back to the sender of a packet that triggered an auditable event, because doing so could itself be used for denial of service.
sections.plainLanguage: Fragments do not carry all the fields the policy database uses, so the RFC defines three safe ways to handle them, including carrying all fragments on one tunnel association and tracking fragments statefully. Protected packets also grow larger, so each association tracks the largest packet the path can carry. The RFC also lists events worth logging, such as a dropped ICMP error that failed its checks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security permeates the whole specification. IPsec imposes strict limits on what header data may pass across the boundary in either direction, particularly with tunnel mode. Outbound, the limits reduce covert channel bandwidth. Inbound, they stop an attacker who can tamper with one data stream on the unprotected side from harming other streams on the protected side.

The RFC gives one concrete warning about ICMP error messages. Suppose sites A, B and C are connected by ESP tunnels whose selectors specify ANY for protocol and ports. If ICMP errors are passed over SAs based on the ICMP header alone, a host at site B could send a Destination Unreachable message declaring all hosts at site C unreachable. That is an efficient denial-of-service attack, and the checks described for ICMP error handling prevent it when the SPD is configured suitably.

The differences from RFC 2401 are mostly changes of detail and organization, but they matter for security. Nested SAs and SA bundles are no longer required; SPD and forwarding tables achieve the same effect. SPD entries now carry lists of ranges. TOS and Traffic Class were replaced by DSCP and ECN. Support for AH is no longer required. Transport mode may now be used between gateways, and between a gateway and a host. ICMP message type and code and the Mobility Header type were added as selectors, and the selector data sensitivity level was removed.
sections.plainLanguage: The main risks come from what the boundary lets through. Header fields copied across the boundary can leak information, and a loose ICMP policy can be turned into a denial-of-service attack. The RFC therefore limits which fields may cross and requires error messages to be checked against the packet that caused them.
